title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Page 382 of E410 (Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 15, 1771) finishes the introduction and states the governing problem.

1. Programme. On the previous page Euler said that the theory of flexible surfaces and bodies is still far off: even its first principles have not been worked out, and so-called theories of sails and linen reduce to the single-thread case. He therefore restricts himself to simple threads, either perfectly flexible or elastic. Existing solutions, he says, rest on special principles or on principles not clearly stated. He promises 'true and general principles' that will settle both equilibrium and motion. In modern terms this is a programme for the one-dimensional continuum (string or rod) built from a single general principle rather than case-by-case tricks.

2. General problem. A thread, perfectly flexible or elastic, is acted on at every point by arbitrary forces and is in equilibrium. Find, for each element, its state of tension or of bending. In modern terms: determine the internal contact force (and, for the elastic case, the contact moment) along the curve.

3. Solution, §I. Let the curve AMB be the thread, fixed at A and B and in equilibrium. At every point M there is a definite state of tension or bending. Proof: if the thread were cut at M, the pieces AM and BM would at once take quite different shapes. So while they are joined, some force at M must resist the separation and keep the configuration in equilibrium; that sentence completes on p.383.

4. Continuation (pp.383ff). Remove AM and ask what load applied at M keeps BM unchanged. This is the method of sections: an imaginary cut, with the removed part replaced by an equivalent contact action. Euler then adds the remark that fixing the thread at intermediate points, even at the neighbouring point m, does not change the required action at M. This localises the internal action to the point itself. It is the conceptual seed of the stress principle for rods: internal force N and couple M at each section, satisfying balance equations of the form dN/ds + f = 0 and dM/ds + t × N + l = 0.

ideas.what: Statement that a general theory of flexible and elastic surfaces and three-dimensional bodies is lacking, even in its first principles; restriction to threads
ideas.modern_name: Programme for 2D/3D continuum mechanics (shells, plates, elastic solids)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Later development by Euler himself (plates, 1766 vibrating bell/membrane), Jakob II Bernoulli (plates, 1789), Sophie Germain/Lagrange (plates), Cauchy (1822-23)
ideas.where_published: E410 introduction; Truesdell's commentary in Opera omnia II.11(2) discusses it

ideas.what: Cutting principle: the existence of an internal action at M is inferred from the change of shape that would follow a cut; the removed part is replaced by forces at the section
ideas.modern_name: Method of sections / precursor of the Euler–Cauchy stress (cut) principle for rods; contact force and contact couple
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (rods, 1770s; E410 and later E481); Cauchy (3D stress, 1822); earlier partial uses by Jacob Bernoulli and others
ideas.where_published: E410; analysed in Truesdell, 'The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638-1788' (Opera omnia II.11(2), 1960)

ideas.what: Unified treatment of perfectly flexible and elastic threads, for equilibrium and motion, from one principle
ideas.modern_name: General balance laws for one-dimensional continua (string/rod theory)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E410, E481); systematised by Truesdell, Antman
ideas.where_published: E410 and related papers on flexible and elastic lines

deep.surprise_reason: This page holds only the introductory programme, the problem statement and the opening of the method of sections. Truesdell analysed E410 in detail and credits it as a key step toward the cut principle, so nothing here is absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: 'satis clarit et perspicuis' should read 'satis claris et perspicuis'.
In the problem statement the line break falls after 'in singulis' / 'sin-gulis'. The transcription 'in singulis punctis' is correct; the image shows 'in sin-' / 'gulis'.
